item.content:encoded:
The Smithsonian Institution is inviting educators to apply for the Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange (DiDVE) Spring 2027 Cohort, an innovative professional development and civic learning opportunity designed to connect students and educators across communities in the United States.

The program, themed “Innovation: A Journey of Civic Imagination,” explores the relationship between innovation, community stories, civic participation, and democracy. Through a combination of virtual exchange, local inquiry, Smithsonian collections, object-based learning, design thinking, and civic discourse, participating educators will guide young people in examining how innovation has shaped communities and contributed to the ongoing democratic story.

Selected facilitators will receive extensive professional support, participate in a three-day training with Smithsonian education leaders in Washington, D.C. with travel and accommodation covered, collaborate with educators from other parts of the country, and receive a $1,500 honorarium upon successful completion of the program.

The application period for the Spring 2027 Cohort opens on August 31, 2026, and closes on October 5, 2026.

About the Smithsonian Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange

Democracy is not simply shaped through national institutions and major political events. It is also influenced by the everyday actions, ideas, traditions, innovations, and collaborations that take place within communities.

The Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange program encourages educators and students to explore these connections by asking important questions about their communities and the role that innovation plays in shaping civic life.

The central theme for the 2026–2027 program is:

Innovation: A Journey of Civic Imagination

Every community contains stories of people who recognized opportunities, responded creatively to challenges, developed new ideas, and imagined better possibilities for the future.

These stories may involve:

  • Technological advancements;
  • Cultural developments;
  • Community-led initiatives;
  • Local traditions;
  • Creative problem-solving;
  • Social movements;
  • New ways of organizing communities;
  • Everyday inventions and innovations;
  • Historical turning points;
  • Ideas that transformed the lives of individuals and communities.

The program encourages students to understand that innovation is closely connected to democracy. When people identify challenges, exchange ideas, collaborate with others, and work toward solutions, they are practicing important civic habits.

Through this process, students can develop a stronger understanding of how communities evolve and how individuals can contribute to shaping the future.

The Guiding Question of the Program

The Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange is built around an important civic inquiry:

In what ways has innovation, large or small, shaped our communities? And how does it help us understand our role in the ongoing American democratic story?

This question provides a framework for educators and students to investigate their communities and explore how historical and contemporary innovations influence people’s lives.

Students will be encouraged to move beyond simply memorizing historical information. Instead, they will engage in active inquiry by examining evidence, considering different perspectives, asking questions, and connecting local experiences with broader national conversations.

What Is the Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange Program?

The Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange is an educational initiative that brings students from different communities together to learn, collaborate, and exchange perspectives.

The program combines local learning with national dialogue.

Students use:

  • Local knowledge;
  • Community stories;
  • Smithsonian collections;
  • Historical objects;
  • Cultural resources;
  • Evidence-based inquiry;
  • Place-based learning;
  • Design thinking;
  • Civic discussion;
  • Collaborative projects.

Through these approaches, participants investigate how innovation has influenced communities and how citizens can participate in shaping society.

One of the distinctive features of the program is that students do not learn in isolation. They connect with peers from other communities, allowing them to compare experiences, exchange perspectives, and discover similarities and differences in how people understand innovation and civic life.

How the Virtual Exchange Works

The program connects educators and students from different locations across the United States.

Participating facilitators partner with another educator from a different area of the country to design and lead a collaborative exchange.

The experience includes both:

1. Asynchronous Learning

Students participate in activities and discussions that do not necessarily require everyone to be online at the same time.

This may allow participants to:

  • Conduct local research;
  • Examine Smithsonian resources;
  • Explore community stories;
  • Complete individual or group assignments;
  • Share reflections;
  • Upload findings;
  • Respond to ideas from students in other communities.

2. Synchronous Learning

Students and facilitators also participate in real-time interactions.

These experiences can help participants:

  • Engage directly with peers;
  • Discuss different perspectives;
  • Present discoveries;
  • Ask questions;
  • Collaborate on ideas;
  • Build relationships across communities;
  • Practice respectful civic dialogue.

By combining both approaches, the program creates a flexible and interactive learning environment that supports meaningful collaboration.

Exploring Innovation Through Civic Imagination

The concept of civic imagination is central to the Democracy in Dialogue program.

Civic imagination encourages individuals to think about the future of their communities and consider how collective action, creativity, and innovation can address challenges.

Participants explore questions such as:

  • How have people in our community responded to challenges?
  • What innovations have transformed the way people live?
  • Who are the individuals behind important local developments?
  • How do traditions influence innovation?
  • What can historical innovations teach us today?
  • How can communities work together to solve current challenges?
  • What role can young people play in shaping the future?
  • How does understanding different perspectives strengthen democracy?

These questions help students see themselves not simply as observers of society, but as individuals who can participate in civic life.

Using Smithsonian Resources for Learning

The Smithsonian Institution provides participants with access to a vast range of educational resources and collections.

Through the program, educators and students explore objects, stories, cultural materials, and historical resources to deepen their understanding of innovation and democracy.

Participants examine how:

  • Technological developments emerge;
  • Cultural changes take place;
  • Communities adapt to new circumstances;
  • Historical experiences influence the present;
  • Everyday ideas can create lasting change;
  • Objects and places contain important stories;
  • Local experiences connect with broader historical narratives.

The use of Smithsonian resources gives students an opportunity to engage with authentic materials while connecting historical knowledge to contemporary civic questions.

Benefits of the Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange 2027

Selected facilitators will receive significant professional and educational benefits through their participation.

1. $1,500 Honorarium

Facilitators who successfully complete the program will receive a $1,500 honorarium.

This recognizes the time, expertise, leadership, and commitment required to guide students through the virtual exchange experience.

2. Fully Supported Three-Day Training

Selected facilitators will attend a three-day training led by Smithsonian education leaders.

The training provides an opportunity to prepare for the program while gaining valuable knowledge and skills related to:

  • Virtual exchange;
  • Civic education;
  • Inquiry-based learning;
  • Dialogue facilitation;
  • Collaborative learning;
  • Community engagement;
  • Object-based learning;
  • Place-based inquiry;
  • Student-centered education.

3. Travel and Accommodation Covered

Participants attending the D.C. Learning Summit will have their travel and accommodation expenses covered.

This significantly reduces the financial barriers associated with participating in the in-person professional development component of the program.

The Learning Summit is scheduled to take place from:

January 11–13, 2027

in Washington, D.C.

4. Professional Development Opportunities

The program provides educators with an opportunity to strengthen their professional practice.

Participants can gain experience in areas such as:

  • Facilitating virtual learning;
  • Designing collaborative educational experiences;
  • Civic discourse;
  • Student engagement;
  • Cross-community learning;
  • Project-based learning;
  • Design thinking;
  • Evidence-based inquiry;
  • Community-centered education.

These skills can also be valuable beyond the duration of the Democracy in Dialogue program.

5. Collaboration With Educators From Other Communities

Participants will partner with another facilitator from a different area of the country.

This provides an opportunity to:

  • Exchange teaching practices;
  • Develop collaborative learning activities;
  • Explore different community perspectives;
  • Build professional relationships;
  • Learn from educators with different experiences;
  • Create meaningful cross-community educational experiences.

6. National Student Connections

Students participating in the program will have the opportunity to connect with peers from other communities.

This can help young people:

  • Develop communication skills;
  • Understand diverse perspectives;
  • Build friendships;
  • Explore different communities;
  • Practice collaboration;
  • Strengthen empathy;
  • Develop civic awareness.

7. Ongoing Professional Support

Facilitators are not expected to manage the program independently.

Program Co-Leads provide support throughout the semester to help ensure that facilitators can successfully implement the exchange.

Participants will also attend regular virtual meetings with other facilitators.

These meetings provide opportunities for:

  • Peer learning;
  • Troubleshooting;
  • Sharing experiences;
  • Professional reflection;
  • Collaborative problem-solving;
  • Ongoing program support.

2026–2027 Democracy in Dialogue Schedule

The Democracy in Dialogue program is organized around semester-based cohorts.

Current Cohort: Fall 2026

Program Period: September–December 2026

Upcoming Cohort: Spring 2027

Program Period: January–May 2027

Important Dates

Activity Date
Application Opens August 31, 2026
Application Deadline October 5, 2026
D.C. Learning Summit January 11–13, 2027
Spring 2027 Program January–May 2027

Applicants interested in joining the Spring 2027 cohort should ensure that they are available for the required program activities throughout the semester.

Who Should Apply for the Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange?

The program is open to educators from all disciplines.

Applicants do not need to specialize exclusively in history, civics, or social studies.

Educators from a wide range of academic and professional backgrounds may be able to integrate the program’s themes into their teaching and learning environments.

Potential applicants may include professionals working in areas such as:

  • Social studies;
  • History;
  • Civics;
  • Science;
  • Technology;
  • Arts;
  • Humanities;
  • Language and literature;
  • Cultural education;
  • Community education;
  • Informal learning;
  • Youth development;
  • Interdisciplinary education.

The key requirement is that applicants work with young people aged 10 to 19 years old and have the capacity to facilitate the program.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants should meet the following general requirements:

1. Be an Educator

The opportunity is intended for individual educators working in educational environments.

Applicants may work in:

  • Schools;
  • Community organizations;
  • Youth programs;
  • Informal education settings;
  • Other educational environments.

2. Work With Students Aged 10–19

Applicants must work with young people within the program’s target age range.

The Democracy in Dialogue program is specifically designed for students aged:

10 to 19 years old

3. Be Available Throughout the Semester

The program is implemented over the course of a semester.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to commit time to:

  • Facilitator training;
  • Student recruitment;
  • Program planning;
  • Virtual exchange activities;
  • In-person student meetings;
  • Community engagement;
  • Facilitator meetings;
  • Final student projects.

4. Recruit at Least 15 Students

Each selected facilitator must recruit a minimum of:

15 students

to participate in the virtual exchange activities.

Applicants should therefore consider their ability to recruit, organize, and consistently engage a group of young participants.

5. Be Willing to Collaborate With Another Facilitator

Participants will partner with another facilitator from a different part of the country.

The partnership involves collaboratively designing and leading a virtual exchange experience.

Successful applicants should therefore be comfortable with:

  • Professional collaboration;
  • Shared planning;
  • Communication;
  • Flexibility;
  • Cross-community engagement.

6. Support Student Projects

Facilitators are responsible for ensuring that students successfully complete their final projects.

This requires active mentorship and support throughout the program.

Responsibilities of a Democracy in Dialogue Facilitator

Selected applicants will take on several responsibilities during the program.

Attend the Three-Day Training

Facilitators must participate in training led by Smithsonian education leaders.

The training will help prepare participants for the implementation of the program.

Travel and accommodation are provided for the training component.

Recruit a Minimum of 15 Students

Each facilitator must organize a group of at least 15 students.

These students will participate in the exchange activities throughout the semester.

Partner With Another Facilitator

Participants will work with an educator from another geographical area.

Together, they will design and facilitate learning experiences that connect their respective student groups.

Facilitate Virtual Exchange Activities

The program includes both asynchronous and synchronous learning experiences.

Facilitators will guide students through these activities and support productive engagement.

Organize Regular In-Person Meetings

Each facilitator is responsible for organizing regular meetings with their students.

These meetings may provide opportunities for students to:

  • Discuss ideas;
  • Conduct research;
  • Reflect on learning;
  • Prepare projects;
  • Connect local experiences to broader themes.

Build Community Connections

The program encourages participants to connect learning with the communities around them.

Facilitators may help students explore:

  • Local history;
  • Community stories;
  • Cultural traditions;
  • Innovation;
  • Civic institutions;
  • Local challenges;
  • Community leaders.

Support Final Student Projects

Students are expected to complete final projects as part of the program.

Facilitators will guide students throughout the process and help ensure successful completion.

Participate in Regular Facilitator Meetings

Selected participants will attend virtual meetings with other facilitators.

These meetings provide continuing professional support and opportunities for collaboration.

How to Apply for the Smithsonian Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange 2027

Applicants must submit their application materials in one PDF document.

The materials must be arranged in the required order.

Required Application Documents

Applicants must submit the following:

1. Letter of Interest

The Letter of Interest should be between:

1 and 2 pages maximum

The letter should address the following areas.

Introduce Yourself

Applicants should provide an introduction that helps the selection team understand their professional background and educational role.

Describe Your Educational Philosophy

Applicants should explain their approach to education and learning.

This may include their perspectives on:

  • Student engagement;
  • Collaborative learning;
  • Inquiry;
  • Community education;
  • Civic learning;
  • Inclusive learning environments.

Explain Your Professional Development Goals

Applicants should describe the skills, knowledge, or experiences they hope to gain through participation in the program.

They should also explain how these goals align with Democracy in Dialogue.

Reflect on Your Community

Applicants are encouraged to discuss their community and the characteristics that define it.

The application should consider questions such as:

  • What qualities make your community unique?
  • What stories are important to your community?
  • What is the community’s capacity for engagement?
  • How have innovation and change shaped the area?

Explain the Potential Impact of the Program

Applicants should explain how Democracy in Dialogue could benefit:

  • Their school or organization;
  • Their students;
  • Their broader community.

They should also consider how they might involve:

  • Other educators;
  • Community stakeholders;
  • Local organizations;
  • Additional partners.

2. Current CV or Resume

Applicants must also submit a current curriculum vitae or resume.

The document should not exceed:

Five pages maximum

Applicants should ensure that their CV or resume clearly presents relevant experience, including educational, professional, community engagement, youth development, or facilitation experience.

Required PDF File Name Format

All application materials must be combined into one PDF file.

Applicants should follow the required naming format:

<LAST NAME, First Initial, Cohort 7 APPLICANT>

Following the requested file format can help ensure that application materials are properly organized and identified during the review process.

Where to Send the Application

Completed application documents should be submitted via email.

Applicants should send their PDF file to: OUSE-Rural-Initiatives@si.edu

It is advisable to carefully review the application before submission and ensure that:

  • The Letter of Interest is included;
  • The Letter of Interest does not exceed two pages;
  • The CV or resume does not exceed five pages;
  • All documents are combined into one PDF;
  • Documents are arranged in the required order;
  • The file name follows the specified format;
  • The application is submitted before the deadline.

Application Deadline

The application period for the Democracy in Dialogue Spring 2027 Cohort runs from:

August 31, 2026, to October 5, 2026.

Deadline: October 5, 2026

Interested educators should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their applications.

Preparing a thoughtful Letter of Interest may require time for applicants to reflect on their educational philosophy, professional development goals, community context, and plans for using the program to benefit students and stakeholders.

Why Educators Should Consider Applying

The Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange offers more than traditional professional development.

It gives educators an opportunity to participate in a national learning community while helping students engage with meaningful questions about innovation, community, civic participation, and democracy.

The program may be particularly valuable for educators interested in:

  • Civic education;
  • Student voice;
  • Community engagement;
  • Collaborative learning;
  • Virtual exchange;
  • Interdisciplinary teaching;
  • Inquiry-based education;
  • Project-based learning;
  • Cultural understanding;
  • Professional networking.

Participants also have the opportunity to develop learning experiences that connect local stories with national conversations.

This approach can help students recognize that their communities contain important histories, knowledge, and ideas that deserve exploration and discussion.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Applicants can improve the quality of their application by carefully connecting their experience and goals to the objectives of Democracy in Dialogue.

1. Demonstrate Your Connection to Education

Clearly explain your experience working with young people and describe the educational setting in which you work.

Show that you understand the needs and interests of students aged 10–19.

2. Connect Your Philosophy to Civic Learning

Discuss how your approach to education supports:

  • Critical thinking;
  • Dialogue;
  • Collaboration;
  • Inquiry;
  • Multiple perspectives;
  • Student participation.

3. Highlight Your Community

The program places significant emphasis on community stories.

Applicants should reflect carefully on what makes their community unique.

Consider identifying:

  • Important historical stories;
  • Local innovations;
  • Community challenges;
  • Cultural traditions;
  • Civic initiatives;
  • People who have contributed to change.

4. Show How You Will Engage Students

Demonstrate that you have a realistic plan for recruiting and supporting at least 15 students.

Applicants should show their ability to create an engaging and supportive learning environment.

5. Think Beyond the Classroom

Consider how the program could benefit the wider community.

Strong applications may explain how the program could involve:

  • Families;
  • Community leaders;
  • Local organizations;
  • Cultural institutions;
  • Other educators;
  • Civic stakeholders.

6. Follow Every Application Instruction

Before submitting, carefully check all formatting requirements.

Small details such as page limits, document order, PDF formatting, and file naming should not be overlooked.

To apply send PDF file to: OUSE-Rural-Initiatives@si.edu

About the Organizations Supporting Democracy in Dialogue

The Democracy in Dialogue initiative is supported through the resources and educational expertise of the Smithsonian Institution.

The program is also made possible through generous support from organizations including:

  • Bezos Family Foundation;
  • Andrew Carnegie Foundation.

The support behind the program enables educators and students to participate in meaningful learning experiences that combine historical inquiry, innovation, civic discourse, and community engagement.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Smithsonian Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange 2027.

Conclusion

The Smithsonian Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange Spring 2027 Cohort presents a valuable opportunity for educators who want to expand their professional practice while creating meaningful learning experiences for young people.

By exploring the theme “Innovation: A Journey of Civic Imagination,” participants will help students investigate how communities respond to challenges, develop new ideas, and shape their futures. The program combines Smithsonian educational resources, local inquiry, virtual exchange, collaborative learning, civic dialogue, and community engagement to create a unique educational experience.

Selected facilitators will benefit from professional training, ongoing support, collaboration with educators from other communities, a fully supported Learning Summit in Washington, D.C., and a $1,500 honorarium upon successful completion of the program.

For educators working with students aged 10–19 who are passionate about civic learning, innovation, community stories, and collaborative education, Democracy in Dialogue offers an opportunity to connect classrooms and communities while helping young people develop the skills needed to participate thoughtfully in civic life.

With the application deadline set for October 5, 2026, eligible educators interested in joining the Spring 2027 cohort should begin preparing their Letter of Interest and CV or resume early and ensure that all materials meet the Smithsonian’s submission requirements.

item.content:encoded:
The Paul Hamlyn Foundation (PHF) Teacher Development Fund supports partnerships between schools and arts or cultural organisations that use arts-based approaches to improve teaching, learning and equity for children.

The fund is designed around the belief that high-quality arts-based learning can help create more equitable classrooms where children can learn, participate and thrive.

Funding Amount and Duration

Successful applicants can receive up to £165,000 per application.

Projects are expected to run for two academic years, giving schools and arts organisations sufficient time to develop professional learning, test arts-based approaches in classrooms, evaluate their impact and build sustainable changes in teaching and learning.

What Does the Teacher Development Fund Support?

The fund focuses on developing teachers’ skills and confidence in using arts-based approaches in education. Supported projects should contribute to more equitable learning environments, particularly for pupils experiencing systemic inequity.

The programme aims to:

  • Improve access to learning for pupils experiencing systemic inequity.
  • Strengthen collaboration between schools and arts or cultural organisations.
  • Provide high-quality professional learning for teachers.
  • Enable teachers and artist practitioners to learn from and work alongside one another in classrooms.
  • Build evidence and practical knowledge about how arts-based learning can improve equity.
  • Encourage sustainable improvements in teaching and learning that continue beyond the project period.

Who Can Lead an Application?

Either of the following can act as the lead applicant:

  1. A primary school, or
  2. An arts or cultural organisation.

However, applications must be based on a strong partnership between schools and arts or cultural organisations.

Each project must involve:

  • A minimum of six schools.
  • A maximum of ten schools.
  • At least one arts or cultural organisation.
  • At least two teachers and one senior leader from each participating school, although some flexibility may be available for small or rural schools.

Eligible Schools and Organisations

Participating schools must operate in the state sector and can include:

  • Mainstream primary schools.
  • Specialist SEND settings.
  • Alternative Provision settings.
  • Schools working with primary-age children.

Teachers working with Nursery and Reception classes in primary schools may also be included.

Eligible arts organisations can include:

  • Charities.
  • Community organisations.
  • Social enterprises.
  • Not-for-profit companies active in the arts and culture sector.

What Will Funded Projects Work On?

The Teacher Development Fund expects projects to develop a structured professional learning programme over two academic years.

Key areas include:

  • Equity: Improving learning opportunities and outcomes for pupils.
  • Professional learning: Developing teachers’ knowledge, skills and confidence.
  • Arts-based approaches: Integrating creative and arts-based methods into classroom teaching.
  • Curriculum: Exploring how arts-based approaches can enhance curriculum delivery.
  • Formative evaluation: Learning from the implementation of the project and using evidence to improve practice.
  • Spreading practice: Sharing learning and effective approaches beyond participating schools.
  • Cohort learning: Creating opportunities for participating schools and practitioners to learn together.
  • Community of practice: Building longer-term networks for collaboration and shared learning.

What Makes a Strong Partnership?

The foundation highlights several characteristics associated with effective partnerships and practice.

These include:

  • Anti-racism.
  • Intersectionality.
  • Effective professional learning.
  • Meaningful involvement of school leaders.
  • Strong roles for artist practitioners.
  • Enquiry-driven and reflective practice.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate that the proposed partnership is more than a simple relationship between a funder, school and arts organisation. The partners should be able to show how they will work together, learn together and create meaningful improvements in teaching and learning.

Deadline

The deadline to apply for the Teacher Development Fund is 11 November 2026 at 12 noon.

Applicants should allow sufficient time to establish the required partnerships, develop the project approach, clarify participating schools and prepare the application before the deadline.

How to Apply

Applications are submitted through the Paul Hamlyn Foundation’s application system.

Applicants should also review the foundation’s detailed eligibility guidance and FAQs before applying.

Click HERE to read more and apply.

Conclusion

The Teacher Development Fund provides substantial support for schools and arts or cultural organisations seeking to use arts-based learning to create more equitable educational environments. With funding of up to £165,000, a two-academic-year project period and a strong emphasis on teacher development, partnership working, evaluation and sustainable change, the opportunity is particularly relevant to organisations with established experience in arts education and schools committed to improving outcomes for children experiencing systemic inequity.

Click HERE for more grant opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
The World Bank Group’s Young Professionals Program (YPP) is its flagship leadership development initiative for highly talented individuals who are passionate about global development.

The Young Professionals Program offers a unique opportunity to build technical expertise, gain international experience and contribute to projects that address the world’s most pressing development challenges.

World Bank YPP Highlights

  • Global and competitive selection
  • Initial start at headquarters followed by field rotations in various World Bank Group offices
  • Initial two-year program followed by a five-year contract upon successful performance
  • Working experience across the World Bank, IFC and MIGA through rotations
  • Tailored training in coaching, mentorship and leadership
  • Opportunities to engage with senior leaders and build strategic professional networks
  • Exposure to global operations and diverse development challenges

Program Features

Rotations provide participants with broad exposure to global operations and diverse development challenges, ensuring a well-rounded understanding of the institution’s work.

Beyond rotations, the program emphasizes continuous learning and career acceleration. Participants benefit from tailored leadership and technical training, dedicated mentorship and direct engagement with senior leaders, creating opportunities to build strategic networks and gain insights into high-level decision-making.

Appointment Type: GF-level term appointment

Duration & Contract: The YPP is a 2-year program. Upon successful completion, participants are placed in a role for an additional 5 years based on performance, with the possibility of contract renewal.

World Bank YPP Tracks

Candidates may apply under one of two tracks:

  • Operations
  • Specialized Functions

World Bank YPP Rotations

The program includes three mandatory rotations of 8 months each, structured as follows:

  • One rotation within your primary function and area of expertise
  • One cross-institutional rotation
  • At least one rotation must be based in a country office

World Bank YPP Eligibility Requirements

Education

Applicants must have a minimum graduate-level degree or a higher qualification in a relevant field, completed before the September start date.

Professional Experience

Candidates need 2 to 6 years of professional experience in a related work area.

If you are pursuing a doctorate, full-time doctoral research studies in a relevant field at an accredited institution may count towards the required work experience. The degree must be substantially complete, with all written work submitted before the September start date.

Guinea, Paraguay, Peru, Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Qatar, Romania, Russian Federation, Rwanda, Samoa, San Marino, São Tomé and Príncipe, Saudi Arabia, Senegal, Serbia, Seychelles, Sierra Leone, Language Proficiency

An excellent command of spoken and written English is mandatory. Fluency in additional languages is considered an advantage and may strengthen your application.

Employment Status

You cannot be a current World Bank Group employee at the time of application (including term, open, short-term [ST], and extended-term [ET] appointments). You also must not have a close relative working at the World Bank Group or a spouse in a direct or indirect supervisory relationship.

World Bank YPP 2027 Application Timeline

Portal Opens

September 1, 2026

Application Deadline

September 30, 2026 at 11:59 PM UTC

Late applications will not be considered.

Interviews & Assessments

December 2026 – January 2027

Final Selection Notification

Late January 2027 – Early February 2027

New Cohort Starts

The new World Bank YPP cohort starts in Washington, DC, in September 2027.

Required Documents

Applicants should prepare the following documents:

  • CV/Resume — ideally 1 page, maximum 2 pages
  • Passport Photo Page — confirming birth date and primary nationality
  • Academic Proof — transcript(s) or enrollment letter(s) verifying postgraduate degrees and expected completion dates

World Bank YPP Selection Process

The World Bank Group Young Professionals Program has a highly competitive selection process.

1. Application

September 1–30, 2026

Applications must be submitted by 11:59 PM UTC on September 30.

2. Longlist

October 1–15, 2026

The full applicant list is reviewed, with the top 10% selected for the next stage.

3. Assessment

October 15–31, 2026

Candidates may be invited to virtual interviews, leadership assessments and technical assessments.

4. Interviews

December 2026 – January 2027

Panel interviews and case studies will take place in:

  • Washington, DC & Nairobi in December
  • Paris & Bangkok in January

5. Selection

Candidates undergo a background check, with offers sent in late January 2027.

6. Entrance

The new cohort begins in September 2027 in Washington, DC.

Is There an Age Requirement for the World Bank YPP?

There is no age requirement for the WBG YPP. However, the program is designed for early-career professionals, so candidates must have 2 to 6 years of relevant professional experience to be eligible.

What Can Successful YPP Candidates Expect?

Successful participants can expect a combination of:

  • International professional experience
  • Cross-institutional exposure
  • Technical and leadership training
  • Coaching and mentorship
  • Career development support
  • Engagement with senior World Bank Group leaders
  • Opportunities to build strategic professional networks
  • Experience working on global development challenges

The program is designed to help exceptional early-career professionals accelerate their careers while contributing to the World Bank Group’s global development mission.

Who Should Apply for the World Bank Young Professionals Program?

The YPP is particularly relevant for talented early-career professionals with a strong interest in global development, international development, economics, finance, public policy, operations, social development and other related fields.

If you have the required graduate-level education, relevant professional experience and a strong interest in tackling global development challenges, the World Bank YPP could be an opportunity worth exploring.

How to Apply for the World Bank YPP

The World Bank Group Young Professionals Program application portal opens on September 1, 2026, and closes on September 30, 2026 at 11:59 PM UTC.

Frequently Asked Questions About the World Bank YPP

Applicants must meet the World Bank Group’s education, professional experience, nationality, language and employment eligibility requirements. Candidates need 2 to 6 years of relevant professional experience and a minimum graduate-level degree or higher qualification in a relevant field.

Is there an age requirement for the WBG YPP?

There is no age requirement. However, candidates must have 2 to 6 years of relevant work experience.

Can current World Bank Group employees apply?

Current World Bank Group employees, including those on term, open, short-term and extended-term appointments, cannot apply at the time of application.

Is the World Bank YPP competitive?

Yes. The program has a highly competitive selection process, with applicants reviewed through multiple stages including longlisting, assessments, interviews and case studies.

When does the 2027 World Bank YPP application open?

The application portal opens on September 1, 2026.

What is the World Bank YPP application deadline?

The deadline is September 30, 2026 at 11:59 PM UTC. Late applications will not be considered.

When does the new World Bank YPP cohort start?

The new cohort is scheduled to start in September 2027 in Washington, DC.

Ready to Explore a Career with the World Bank Group?

item.content:encoded:
World Food Forum Global School Assembly 2026 Registration Open for Schools and Students

Registration is now open for the World Food Forum Global School Assembly 2026, an international educational gathering designed to give school students a meaningful platform to discuss the future of food, agriculture and sustainable agrifood systems.

The Global School Assembly will take place on Tuesday, 13 October 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. CET at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations in Rome, Italy. Schools interested in participating must complete the official registration process by 27 September 2026.

The Assembly will bring students, teachers, educators and school representatives together to exchange experiences, discuss challenges in their local food systems and consider how young people can contribute to the transformation of global agrifood systems.

Key Details of the World Food Forum Global School Assembly 2026

  • Name: World Food Forum – Global School Assembly 2026
  • Event date: Tuesday, 13 October 2026
  • Assembly time: 10:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. CET
  • Location: FAO Headquarters, Rome, Italy
  • Participation: School-based participation
  • Student levels: Primary school, middle school and high school
  • Student ages covered by the form: Approximately 5–18 years
  • Registration deadline: 27 September 2026
  • Travel funding: Participating schools and students must cover their own travel and accommodation expenses
  • Contact email: education@world-food-forum.org
  • Official registration form: World Food Forum Global School Assembly Registration 2026

The registration form does not specify a closing time on the deadline date. Schools are therefore encouraged to complete the process well before 27 September 2026.

About the World Food Forum Global School Assembly

The World Food Forum Global School Assembly is intended to serve as a dialogue platform where students can share their perspectives on the opportunities and challenges affecting agrifood systems in their local communities.

Agrifood systems encompass the complete journey of food, including its production, processing, transportation, marketing, consumption and disposal. These systems affect food security, nutrition, livelihoods, public health, natural resources, climate change and sustainable development.

Students attending the Assembly will be encouraged to bring experiences from their schools and communities into a wider international conversation. The programme seeks to create an environment where knowledge can be exchanged:

  • Between students from different countries and cultural backgrounds
  • Between participating schools and educational institutions
  • Across different age groups and generations
  • Between young people, educators, FAO specialists and participating partners
  • Between local experiences and global agrifood priorities

The Assembly is also expected to reinforce FAO’s role in motivating and supporting students to become active contributors to agrifood systems transformation.

What Students Can Expect from the Assembly

The programme is designed to move beyond a conventional classroom discussion. Students will have an opportunity to reflect on food and agricultural challenges affecting their communities while learning how similar issues are experienced in other parts of the world.

The main areas of engagement include:

1. Student-Led Dialogue

Students will be given space to express their views on the challenges and opportunities they observe in their local agrifood systems. Depending on their context, these may include food waste, access to healthy food, environmental sustainability, nutrition, agricultural production, climate change, water management or community awareness.

2. International Knowledge Exchange

The Assembly aims to connect students from different countries and educational backgrounds. This international dimension can help students understand that food-system challenges are global, although their causes and consequences may differ between communities.

3. Intergenerational Learning

The programme is designed to facilitate exchanges not only among students but also across generations. This can create opportunities for young people to learn from educators and specialists while allowing decision-makers and professionals to hear directly from students.

4. Engagement with Agrifood Systems Transformation

Students will explore how education, youth participation, responsible behaviour and practical local action can contribute to fairer, more inclusive and sustainable agrifood systems.

Discovery Station Tour at FAO Headquarters

Participating schools are required to confirm their participation in an approximately two-hour Discovery Station Tour.

The Discovery Station Tour is described as an interactive experience in which students rotate in small groups between educational stations operated by different FAO divisions and partner organizations.

Important features of the tour include:

  • Students will be placed in groups of approximately 20 participants.
  • Each group will be guided by an FAO chaperone.
  • Groups will rotate between several Discovery Stations.
  • Each individual station activity will last approximately 20–25 minutes.
  • Activities will be designed to be engaging, educational and suitable for students.
  • The stations will demonstrate the diverse areas of expertise within FAO and their connection to food and agriculture.
  • A scheduled break will be included so that students can eat their packed lunches.

Schools should accordingly plan for the Assembly session and an additional approximately two-hour Discovery Station Tour. The registration form does not provide a separate start or finishing time for the tour, so registered schools should obtain the final schedule from the organizing team.

Important Clarification About In-Person and Online Participation

The Microsoft registration form identifies FAO Headquarters in Rome as the event venue and requires schools to confirm that they will cover their own travel and accommodation expenses. It also requires confirmation of participation in the in-person Discovery Station Tour.

However, the official World Food Forum CultivatED page explains that schools in Italy are invited to attend the Global School Assembly in Rome, while schools outside Italy join online.

International schools should therefore contact education@world-food-forum.org before booking flights or accommodation to confirm whether they should participate online or whether they may register an in-person delegation through this form.

Information Schools Must Provide in the Registration Form

The registration process is completed by a designated school contact person. The form explains that the school contact person is the individual completing and submitting the registration.

Schools should prepare the following information:

School Contact Information

The form requires:

  • Full name of the school contact person
  • Role of the contact person
  • Contact person’s email address
  • Name of the school
  • Full school address, including street number, city, province and postal code
  • Country in which the school is located

The available role options include:

  • Head teacher
  • Head teacher alternate
  • Teacher
  • Secretary
  • Other authorized role

School Level and Student Age Groups

Schools must indicate whether they are registering as a:

  • Primary school
  • Middle school
  • High school

The form allows schools to select the relevant student year groups and age ranges:

  • Year 1: ages 5–6
  • Year 2: ages 6–7
  • Year 3: ages 7–8
  • Year 4: ages 8–9
  • Year 5: ages 9–10
  • Year 6: ages 10–11
  • Year 7: ages 11–12
  • Year 8: ages 12–13
  • Year 9: ages 13–14
  • Year 10: ages 14–15
  • Year 11: ages 15–16
  • Year 12: ages 16–17
  • Year 13: ages 17–18

Schools may select more than one relevant year or age group.

Number of Participants

Applicants must provide:

  • Total number of participating school staff and parents
  • Total number of participating students

Schools should confirm their proposed delegation before starting the application so that the numbers entered in the form correspond with the names provided in the attendee list.

Mandatory Attendee List

Every school must download the Excel attendee-list template provided inside the registration form.

The school must then:

  1. Download a copy of the official Excel file.
  2. Complete the file with the names of all participants from the school.
  3. Check that the participant names and total numbers are accurate.
  4. Upload the completed file to Google Drive.
  5. Change its sharing settings so that “Anyone with the link” can access it.
  6. Copy the Google Drive sharing link.
  7. Paste that link into the relevant field in the Microsoft registration form.

A restricted Google Drive link could prevent the organizing team from accessing the attendee information. Schools should test the link in a private browser window or while signed out of Google before submitting the registration.

The official attendee-list template can be accessed through the link embedded in the Microsoft registration form.

Parental Consent for Photography and Videography

The Assembly requires parental or legal-guardian consent for the photography and videography of participating minor students.

Schools must use the Parental Consent Form provided inside the registration form and complete the following actions:

  1. Download a copy of the official Parental Consent Form.
  2. Provide the form to the parents or legal guardians of every participating minor.
  3. Ensure that every required form is properly completed and signed.
  4. Retain all signed copies in the school’s records.
  5. Confirm that the signed forms will have been collected by the date of the Global School Assembly.
  6. Acknowledge that the World Food Forum Global Youth Action Initiative may request copies of the signed consent forms at any time during the one-year period following the event.

Schools should establish a clear consent-tracking system and keep the signed records securely for at least the period during which the organizers may request them.

The Parental Consent Form is available through the official Microsoft registration form.

Travel, Accommodation and Other Costs

The registration form requires schools to confirm that the school and/or participating students will be responsible for paying their own travel and accommodation expenses for attendance in Rome.

The form does not announce:

  • Travel grants
  • Accommodation support
  • Airfare reimbursement
  • Visa sponsorship
  • Daily allowances
  • Meal allowances
  • Financial assistance for accompanying staff or parents

Schools should not assume that FAO or the World Food Forum will reimburse any participation costs.

Before making travel commitments, international schools should confirm:

  • Their approved participation format
  • Whether their delegation will attend in person or online
  • Final attendance confirmation
  • Visa requirements for Italy
  • Travel dates and accommodation arrangements
  • Local transportation in Rome
  • Insurance and safeguarding arrangements
  • Lunch and refreshment arrangements for students
  • Any access requirements at FAO Headquarters

Accessibility and Support for Students

The World Food Forum Global School Assembly explicitly welcomes students with special educational or accessibility needs.

The form describes diversity as an important part of inclusion, dialogue and mutual learning. It states that specific measures will be considered to help provide an accessible, safe and positive experience for participating students.

Schools are invited to report needs such as:

  • Reduced mobility
  • Visual impairment
  • Hearing disability
  • Individual support requirements
  • Alternative communication tools
  • Neurodevelopmental conditions, including autism, ADHD or specific learning disabilities
  • Other accessibility or educational support needs

If any participating student requires assistance, the school must provide:

  • The number of students requiring support
  • A detailed description of the assistance needed
  • Confirmation of whether a support assistant or educator will attend
  • The full name of the support educator, where applicable
  • Details of any tools or aids that the student will bring
  • The applicable type of need or disability

Examples of tools and aids mentioned in the form include:

  • Wheelchairs
  • Canes
  • Specific software
  • Tablets
  • Hearing aids

This information will help the organizing team arrange an appropriate and personalized welcome. The stated objective is to enable every student to participate fully in both the Global School Assembly and the Discovery Station Tour.

Schools should provide clear, practical information without withholding arrangements that may be necessary for student safety or participation.

Data Protection and Privacy

Applicants must accept the FAO Data Protection and Privacy Notice before continuing with the registration.

According to the notice contained in the form, FAO collects and processes personal information to:

  • Assess registrations or applications
  • Facilitate participation in projects under the WFF Youth Initiative
  • Support project and activity implementation
  • Communicate effectively with participating schools
  • Coordinate collaboration among participants
  • Support capacity-development activities
  • Contribute to the effective implementation of the initiative

FAO states that personal information will be treated confidentially and will not be shared with persons or organizations outside FAO without specific consent, except where selected and duly authorized partners or service providers support FAO or collaborate with it.

FAO also states that it seeks to ensure that authorized third parties maintain data-protection safeguards comparable to those applied by FAO. Personal data will be retained only for as long as necessary for the purposes described in the notice and in accordance with FAO rules.

The Microsoft form does not automatically collect a respondent’s name and email address unless these are entered. However, the registration itself requires the school contact person to provide both their name and email address.

Applicants can read the complete FAO Data Protection and Privacy Notice. Questions concerning the processing of personal data may be directed to FAO-Data-Privacy@fao.org.

Final Questions in the Registration Form

Before submitting the form, applicants must indicate how they learned about the Global School Assembly. Available responses include:

  • FAO website
  • World Food Forum website
  • Word of mouth
  • A friend or colleague
  • Other source

The form also provides an optional field where schools can enter additional notes, requests or special requests for the organizing team.

Schools should use this field to communicate important matters that are not adequately covered elsewhere in the registration, particularly logistical, safeguarding, accessibility or participation-related questions.

How to Complete the Application

Schools can follow these steps:

  1. Identify an authorized school contact person.
  2. Confirm the proposed number of students, staff and accompanying parents.
  3. Determine the participating students’ school years and age ranges.
  4. Open the official Microsoft registration form.
  5. Read and accept the FAO Data Protection and Privacy Notice.
  6. Enter the school and contact-person information.
  7. Select the school grade and applicable student age groups.
  8. Download and complete the attendee-list Excel file.
  9. Upload the completed attendee list to Google Drive.
  10. Set access to “Anyone with the link.”
  11. Obtain signed parental consent forms for all participating minors.
  12. Confirm participation in the Discovery Station Tour.
  13. Confirm responsibility for travel and accommodation costs.
  14. Provide full details of any accessibility or educational support needs.
  15. Add any final notes or special requests.
  16. Review all information and submit the registration by 27 September 2026.

Practical Advice for Schools

Before submitting, schools should verify that:

  • The contact email address is accurate and regularly monitored.
  • The school address includes all requested components.
  • Participant numbers agree with the attendee list.
  • Every name in the attendee list is correctly spelled.
  • The Google Drive file opens without requesting access.
  • Parents or legal guardians understand the photography and videography consent requirements.
  • Signed consent forms are stored securely.
  • Support and accessibility information is complete.
  • Travel funding has not been assumed.
  • International participation arrangements have been confirmed directly with the organizers.
  • A copy or screenshot of the completed registration is retained for school records.

Registration Deadline

The deadline to complete the registration is:

27 September 2026

Schools are strongly advised not to wait until the final day. Preparing the attendee list, obtaining parental consent and confirming accessibility requirements may require coordination among teachers, parents, administrators and students.

Application and Reference Link

Complete the official registration through the Microsoft Cloud form:

Apply for the World Food Forum Global School Assembly 2026

For questions about registration, participation arrangements or the event programme, contact education@world-food-forum.org.

Conclusion

The World Food Forum Global School Assembly 2026 offers schools an opportunity to bring students into an international discussion about food, agriculture, sustainability and the future of agrifood systems.

Through student dialogue, international knowledge exchange, intergenerational engagement and interactive Discovery Stations, the programme seeks to help young people understand global challenges while contributing perspectives from their own schools and communities.

Participation requires careful preparation. Schools must compile an accurate attendee list, obtain consent for participating minors, disclose accessibility requirements, confirm participation in the Discovery Station Tour and understand that travel and accommodation expenses are not covered by the organizers.

Interested schools should begin coordinating their delegations immediately and complete the official registration no later than 27 September 2026.
